news.content:
The three-month correlation between Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) and the Nasdaq 100 has dropped to -0.12, establishing an inverse correlation. Financial commentary publication The Kobeissi Letter stated this marks the metric “turning negative for the first time on record in data going back to the early 1980s.”

Historic Negative Correlation

The Kobeissi Letter reports that the correlation between Apple and the Nasdaq 100 has remained negative for two consecutive months. During this timeframe, Apple shares gained 9.7%, while the broader Nasdaq 100 index increased by 0.2%.

To provide historical context, the publication stated that in June 2025, the correlation stood at +0.90. Furthermore, between 2006 and 2025, the correlation never fell below +0.30. The Kobeissi Letter concluded that this divergence between Apple and the rest of the technology sector is “unprecedented.”

Read Also: Steve Jobs Thought They Were ‘Ergonomically Terrible,’ but Apple Is Reportedly Betting You’ll Pay a Premium for the Touchscreen MacBook Pro

Closing the Valuation Gap

Alongside this decoupling, financial research platform Trading Terminal observed a sudden shift in tech valuations. According to Trading Terminal, the market capitalization gap between Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Apple shrank from $903 billion on Oct. 6 to $181 billion within three weeks, erasing 80% of the difference.

During this span, Apple added approximately $197 billion in market value, whereas Nvidia lost approximately $525 billion. Co-founder and CTO of Trading Terminal, Andrew Aziz questioned this shift, asking, “Are investors suddenly preferring Apple’s predictable steady cash flows over the volatile AI infrastructure?”

Investor Flight to Safety

Trading Terminal attributed the rapid valuation shift to investors rotating toward Apple’s “predictable iPhone and Services cash flows.” The platform noted that Nvidia was pressured by “AI infrastructure debt, circular financing and hyperscaler return concerns.”

Trading Terminal also highlighted the valuation disparity, arguing that Apple trades at a roughly 43% higher earnings multiple despite Nvidia’s substantially faster revenue growth. The platform characterized the movement as a “massive divergence in what investors currently view as safe.”

Noting Apple and Nvidia report earnings on Nov. 2 and Nov. 17, respectively, Trading Terminal stated the valuation winner “may be determined by which company the market fears less, not which company grows faster.”

How Has AAPL Performed in 2026?

The stock was higher by 29.12% over the last year, up 27.68% year-to-date, and higher by 1.77% over the last month. The stock closed up 0.93% at $347.10 on Tuesday.

Benzinga’s Edge Stock Rankings indicate that AAPL maintains a positive price trend in the short, long, and medium terms, with a moderate growth score.

news.content:
Investor Kevin O’Leary urged investors to limit their exposure to individual stocks and sectors, saying diversification helped shape his returns after earlier investing losses.

O’Leary Shares His 5% Stock Investment Rule

On Tuesday, in a post on X, O’Leary warned that investors often become emotionally attached to companies, leading them to overlook the risks of concentrating their portfolios in a few stocks.

"Even to the greatest names, there are massive corrections on sectoral transitions," he wrote, noting that investors cannot predict where they are in a market cycle.

O’Leary recommended investing no more than 5% of a portfolio in any one stock and capping exposure to any single sector at 20%.

"My returns are based on this concept of diversification, although if you looked at what I was doing 20 years ago, I wasn’t applying those rules and I got slaughtered," he said.

Nvidia and Tech Stocks Face Diversification Test

In a clip, O’Leary explained that investors can become so enthusiastic about a company that they continue buying its shares whenever prices fall.

He used Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) as an example, saying the stock should never account for more than 5% of a portfolio, while the entire technology sector should remain capped at 20%.

O’Leary said diversification encourages investors to explore other industries that may be out of favor but could eventually recover.

He also acknowledged that he had failed to follow the approach earlier in his career.

Read Also: Kevin O’Leary Offered This Entrepreneur $700,000 On ‘Shark Tank.’ He Turned It Down — Then Amazon Bought The Company For $1B

Experts Warn Investors About S&P 500 Concentration Risk

Earlier this month, Nvidia, Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) accounted for more than 21% of the S&P 500, raising concerns about concentration risk for investors in market-cap-weighted ETFs.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP) offered an alternative by assigning roughly equal weights to companies in the index.

In July, Jim Cramer warned investors against excessive technology exposure amid volatility in AI stocks, urging them to explore other sectors despite his long-term confidence in Nvidia and Intel.

In January, O’Leary also urged young investors to diversify, recommending that they limit exposure to 5% in any single stock and 20% in any sector to reduce risk during market downturns.

news.author: Chris Katje
news.content:
Based on more than 50 years of stock trading in the U.S., one day has to be the best day for investors. That day happens to be today, Oct. 28, with an average daily gain of 0.50% dating back to 1950.

This year’s best day could be spoiled by a major event.

Best Trading Day of the Year

For many years, Oct. 28 has been known as the historical best trading day for the S&P 500, which is tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY).

Carson Group Chief Market Strategist Ryan Detrick, who is well-known on social media for his charts and historical trading patterns, highlighted the day earlier this week and why 2026 is different.

"Something has to give, as October 28th is historically the best day of the year. This day falls on this Wednesday and that is also a Fed meeting. Under Kevin Warsh we’ve seen the S&P 500 fall 1.21% in June, 1.52% in July and 0.45% in September. Which history will repeat?" Detrick tweeted.

Those declines refer to the dates of the Federal Reserve meetings, led by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh in those respective months.

"In other words, when Warsh talks, the market hasn’t liked it, but tomorrow is usually a good day. Time to buckle up!" Detrick said in a blog post.

The Federal Reserve is expected to hold rates steady on Wednesday. A decision to cut or raise rates could create high volatility for a market that has not priced in either of those outcomes. Even without a rate change, the markets could trade uneasily on Wednesday.

While there is no guarantee that Oct. 28 will be the best trading day each year, or have a positive return each year, the 2026 calendar could come with an asterisk due to it also being a Fed day.

A chart shared by Detrick shows that Oct. 28, which is also the market expert’s birthday, is the best date based on average returns since 1950.

The date beats out Dec. 26 and April 9, which have average gains of 0.48% and 0.44%, respectively.

On the other side of the spectrum is Oct. 19, which is the worst day of the year, with an average decline of 0.52% since 1950. This year, Oct. 19 saw a modest 0.4% gain for the S&P 500.

Read Also: S&P 500 Hits New Highs Ahead of Four-Year Bull Market Anniversary: Market Expert Says ‘Party Isn’t Over Yet’

Fighting Against History

The 2026 market may go down as one of the most unusual, with new highs set despite macroeconomic uncertainties and periods of war.

The S&P 500 has also fought against historical norms, such as September being the worst month for the index. This year saw a modest gain for September.

Detrick said investors are heading into the bullish late October period. This comes as a four-year bull market continues on, despite concerns for AI bubbles and other potential negative sentiment.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust is up 12.7% year-to-date in 2026 and on pace for a fifth straight year of double-digit returns for investors.

news.content: Cloudera has launched Cloudera Blueprints, a platform designed to simplify the deployment of AI at scale by integrating NVIDIA's AI software stack with Cloudera's hybrid data platform. The integration allows organizations to leverage NVIDIA NIM microservices, NVIDIA Nemotron models, and NVIDIA cuDF for Apache Spark to accelerate data preparation and inference workloads. This collaboration is intended to help enterprises move AI prototypes into production-ready applications by providing secure data management and governance. The initiative aims to reduce vendor lock-in and provide flexibility for deploying AI models across cloud, on-premises, and edge environments.

news.content: Otto Group and Sereact are implementing a two-phase project to automate the complex task of processing e-commerce returns using AI-controlled robotic systems. The initiative will initially deploy ten dual-arm robotic systems at Otto Group's logistics center in Poland, with plans to scale to 25 units in a second phase based on performance results. The robots utilize NVIDIA's technology to handle the variability of returned items, which are often crumpled or repackaged, a task that has historically been difficult to automate. This project aims to improve supply chain flexibility and resilience by applying Physical AI to real-world logistics challenges.

news.author: Jeannine Mancini
news.content:
Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) founder Jeff Bezos won’t call the top of the AI boom, but he knows exactly what he’d tell someone living off their savings.

Fox News host Bret Baier asked Bezos whether the industry is in a bubble. “It’s hard to know,” Bezos said in an interview on Oct. 7. “What I do know is the technology is real.”

Good Ideas, Bad Ideas, Same Funding Round

Bezos said the trouble is that in these periods “every experiment gets funded, the good ideas and the bad ideas.” He added that “in the moment, in all of the tussle of this, it’s hard for investors to know the difference between the good ideas and the bad ideas.”

Speculators can lose money when enthusiasm runs ahead of results, he said, but the inventions themselves don’t disappear. In his view, that dynamic is “tricky for investors” and “good for society.”

The Math That Makes The Line Blurry

The numbers show why the call is hard to make. A JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM) basket of 41 AI-linked companies has accounted for roughly 49% of the S&P 500’s market value, a concentration not seen for a single theme since the railroads. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) carry heavy index weights on their own.

The five largest hyperscalers are guiding toward roughly $800 billion in 2026 capital spending on AI infrastructure, while the cleanest measures of above-trend AI-related revenue remain a fraction of that. Spending is real and accelerating, but the full payoff is not yet visible.

Own The Whole Market, Skip The Contest

Then Baier asked the practical question. “Would you tell a retiree to own AI stocks today?”

“I would usually tell a retiree to buy the S&P 500,” Bezos said.

“Play it safe,” Baier replied.

The S&P 500 is the broad, low-cost default that already owns the major AI companies in proportion to their size. Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRK)(NYSE:BRK) Chairman Emeritus Warren Buffett and other long-term investors have given the same advice for decades, which is to own the market and skip the stock-picking contest. For a retiree, that is the simplest way to stay invested without trying to separate the good experiments from the bad ones while the tussle is still underway.

SK hynix Inc. (NASDAQ:SKHY) now turns 80% of its sales into operating profit. Yet even after Wednesday’s rally, its Seoul-listed shares are worth about half what they were in June.

The memory maker posted record third-quarter results on Wednesday, and the stock jumped 10.9% to 1,487,000 won, its biggest one-day gain since July 31.

Still, that leaves the shares 49% below their record close of 2,919,000 won on June 22. Between Sept. 1 and Tuesday, they had lost 21% as investors questioned how long Big Tech’s artificial-intelligence spending could last.

MS Hwang, research director at Counterpoint Research, told Benzinga the memory boom has further to run.

“Pricing power is highly likely to remain in the hands of suppliers for the next several years,” Hwang said.

Yet, he expects Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. (OTC:SSNLF) to lead in the most valuable part of the market by 2027.

SK hynix daily chart and daily rate of change. Source: TradingView

According to Hwang, Samsung spent too long on the chip-scaling race and was slow to build products for AI customers. Still, he expects the Suwon, South Korea-based tech company to overtake SK hynix starting with HBM4 and lead in market share by 2027.

“The new management team’s choice was a ‘back to basics’, sacrificing immediate market share to ensure the quality of products delivered to clients,” Hwang said. “Although this transition took time, it has proven successful.”

Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU), a late entrant in HBM, is steadily moving toward an HBM share that matches its overall position in memory, he added.

A Quarter That Topped 100 Trillion Won

SK hynix’s operating profit reached 83.3 trillion won, or about $62.2 billion. That’s up from 11.4 trillion won a year earlier. Analysts had expected about 77 trillion won, Hwang noted.

Revenue rose 328% to 104.6 trillion won ($78 billion), above 100 trillion won for the first time.

The company also plans about 100 trillion won ($74.6 billion) in shareholder returns this year, including a 20,000-won third-quarter dividend.

Hwang welcomed the decision to drop a planned IPO of Solidigm, its NAND storage unit.

“If the returns do not flow back to shareholders, it is hard to re-rate the stock,” he said in emailed comments.

Read Also: Nvidia's Credit Risk Has Tripled This Year — and Just Passed Meta's

Nvidia’s Rubin Ramp Clears a Key Hurdle

For months, the main worry was whether SK hynix could qualify HBM4, its newest high-bandwidth memory, for Nvidia Corp.‘s (NASDAQ:NVDA) next-generation Rubin platform.

“While challenges were anticipated through September, supply is now fortunately expected to proceed without a hitch,” Hwang told Benzinga.

According to Hwang, both sides gave ground. Nvidia lowered its maximum pin speed from 11.7 to 10.6 gigabits per second, while SK hynix improved its manufacturing yields.

Prices Could Fall 30% and Margins Would Still Be Huge

Hwang argued that memory earnings are now driven by pricing rather than volume. Prices that sat around 20 to 30 cents per gigabit have climbed to about $2, he said, and HBM4 should reach $4.

That lifted the DRAM market above $200 billion in a single quarter for the first time, according to Hwang.

“Even if prices drop by 30% in 2028, suppliers’ profit margins would arithmetically only ease from 80% to 70% level,” he said.

Q3 Figures Back That Up

A 30% revenue cut with flat costs would still leave about 51.9 trillion won ($38.8 billion) in operating profit, a 71% margin.

SK hynix has also signed long-term agreements covering more than half of its 2027 and 2028 capacity.

Cantor Fitzgerald’s C.J. Muse, who rates the stock Overweight with a $250 target, said the shares trade at about three times his 2027 earnings estimate.

“Our view is this current AI cycle is elongated and durable, supported by TSMC/HBM/Substrate constraints,” Muse said.

One detail in his note stands out. Cantor estimates that conventional DRAM reached gross margins of about 90% in the September quarter, above the roughly 78% earned on HBM.

Net profit, however, fell 58% from the second quarter on currency and investment losses, Muse noted.

Read Also: Nasdaq 100 Climbs on Chip Rally, Boeing Sinks 10%: Stock Market Today

Why a 2018-Style Order Freeze Looks Unlikely

In the worst case, Hwang says, a 2018-style pullback could see cloud providers cut orders at once.

“To enable full-fledged AI services, memory has essentially become a utility cost,” Hwang said. Barring a macro shock, a synchronized halt in orders is “highly unlikely,” he added.

For U.S. investors, the Roundhill Memory ETF (BATS:DRAM), which holds Micron, Samsung and SK hynix, is up 73% since its April debut.

SK hynix has shown that the profits are real. What the market has yet to price is how long they last and how much Samsung wins back.

Editor’s Note: The ETFs tracking benchmark indices, lede, economic data, and the headline were updated in the story.

U.S. stocks were higher on Wednesday, as the Dow Jones, S&P 500, and Nasdaq 100 index futures rose, following Tuesday’s higher close.

The U.S. advance international trade deficit in goods widened to $134.9 billion in September 2026, marking a $2.8 billion increase from August. Alongside the trade data, advance estimates for September showed wholesale inventories rising 0.6% to $1,011.5 billion, while retail inventories increased 0.3% to $885.3 billion.

Investors will watch the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee’s interest rate decision and the monetary policy report later today, with the FOMC press conference scheduled at 2:30 p.m. ET. The CME Group’s FedWatch tool projections show markets pricing in a 90.6% likelihood of interest rates being unchanged.

President Donald Trump said he plans to ban the term “artificial intelligence” from relevant government documents and urged the use of “super intelligence” instead, prompting Rep. Ted Lieu to argue that renaming the technology will not address oversight concerns.

The U.S. military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters, compared with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth‘s July estimate of $37.5 billion. Reuters also reported that more than $29 billion would go to replace expended munitions and more than $6 billion would be needed from Congress for equipment and platform losses.

Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury bond yielded 5.01%, and the 2-year Treasury bond yielded 4.75%, at the last check.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ) and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (NYSE:DIA), which track the S&P 500 index, Nasdaq 100 index and Dow Jones Industrial Average, respectively, were higher in premarket trading on Wednesday. The SPY was up 0.27% at $771.72, the QQQ advanced 0.43% to $724.38, and the DIA rose 0.052% to $523.55.

Cues From Last Session

U.S. stocks closed higher on Tuesday, led by information technology, consumer discretionary, and materials. Energy, consumer staples, and real estate lagged.

Insights From Analysts

Professor Jeremy J. Siegel, senior economist to WisdomTree and emeritus professor of finance at The Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, said last week featured an “extraordinarily sharp rotation out of growth and into value,” with the Russell Value Index and the S&P Value Index reaching all-time highs even as the Nasdaq sold off.

He tied the rotation to uncertainty about the scale and durability of the AI investment boom and said the 10-year Treasury yield moving back below 5% supported bonds and rate-sensitive value stocks.

Siegel wrote, “That is why I continue to view bonds and value stocks as natural hedges against the dominant AI trade,” and added, “The market is no longer trading as one giant AI momentum story.”

He also said this week’s Federal Reserve meeting should be “rather uneventful,” noting there is no Summary of Economic Projections or dot plot and he sees no change in policy.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) reports third-quarter earnings Wednesday, with CEO Sundar Pichai facing a $200 billion question: Is Google’s massive AI spending paying off?

On Kalshi, traders have wagered more than $171,000 on which words Pichai and his team will say during the call.

Analysts expect earnings of about $3.02 per share on revenue near $128 billion, up 25% from a year ago.

Alphabet shares have gained just 2% this year and sit roughly 22% below their May high.

What Kalshi Predicts Google Will Say

“Gemini” leads at 98% for at least three mentions. Google’s flagship AI powers products across Search, Workspace and Cloud, making it central to the company’s competition with OpenAI and Anthropic.

The Gemini app reached 950 million monthly users last quarter, while Google said nearly 90% of Fortune 100 companies use Gemini Enterprise. Investors will be watching whether that adoption translates into revenue.

“AI Mode” follows at 92%. Google’s conversational search feature faces a more immediate financial test: whether AI-powered answers can generate as much advertising revenue as traditional search.

“Nvidia” trades at 84%. Google Cloud rents out Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) GPUs, but its own Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), are emerging as a challenge to Nvidia’s dominance.

Oracle announced Tuesday it will offer Google’s TPUs to cloud customers starting in 2027, potentially expanding Google’s chip business beyond its own cloud platform.

“Wiz” sits at 79%. Google completed its $32 billion acquisition of the cloud security firm in March, expanding its enterprise offering.

“Headwind” is at 76%. CFO Anat Ashkenazi warned that currency movements could weigh on third-quarter Search and YouTube advertising revenue.

"Chrome" trades at 73%. The world’s most popular browser drives traffic to Google’s lucrative Search business and now integrates Gemini, turning it into a key distribution channel for Google’s AI.

A federal judge rejected a forced sale of Chrome last year, but the Justice Department is appealing that decision.

What Kalshi Predicts Google Will Skip

“Regulator,” “Regulation” or “Regulatory” trades at 23%, despite Google’s ongoing legal battles over Search.

“Ironwood” trades at just 16%. Google unveiled its eighth-generation AI chips, TPU 8t and TPU 8i, in April, promising major performance improvements over Ironwood. Traders may expect Pichai to focus on the newer chips instead.

“SpaceX” is at 14%. Alphabet’s stake in Elon Musk’s SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) was worth $94 billion at the end of June, and Google agreed to pay the company $920 million monthly for AI computing capacity.

Reading the Board

Google Cloud revenue is expected to reach $29 billion, nearly double last year’s figure. But keeping up with that demand is becoming increasingly expensive.

Alphabet plans to spend $195 billion to $205 billion on capital investments this year. Bank of America analyst Justin Post sees potential upside from Cloud growth and TPU sales, but estimates spending could climb to $300 billion in 2027.

That’s another $100 billion a year, raising questions about when Google’s AI investments will deliver stronger cash flow.

Pichai needs to show investors not just how fast Google’s AI business is growing, but how much money it can actually make.

news.content:
Market strategists from Carson Research caution that the recent broadening of stock market gains away from technology companies into defensive sectors mirrors the rotation seen during the dot-com bubble, warning investors to “be careful what you wish for.”

Recent Market Divergence

Chief Market Strategist Ryan Detrick and Chief Macro Strategist Sonu Varghese highlighted a recent trading session where the broader index declined while a majority of individual stocks advanced.

Varghese noted that on a recent Thursday, 324 out of 500 S&P 500 stocks gained. However, Varghese stated the S&P 500 fell 1.4%, and technology was down 3.3%.

He stated that the advancing stocks were led by defense, consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare. Addressing the desire for wider market participation beyond technology, Varghese warned, “Be careful what you wish for. You get more breadth, but do you want that to be led by defensives?”

Detrick noted that on the same day, the equal-weight S&P 500 outperformed the capitalization-weighted index by almost 2%. Detrick said it was the “best breadth day on a 1% down day” seen recently.

Emphasizing the necessity of the technology sector, Detrick stated, “You need tech leadership.” Detrick added that technology has been a top-performing sector in almost every bull market over the last 100 years.

Read Also: S&P Changes the Rules – Here's New Value Vs. Growth

Historical Parallels to the Dot-Com Era

Varghese compared the current market conditions to the early 2000s. He stated, “The dot-com bubble… it didn’t end with a bust, right? It ended with rotation.”

According to Varghese, between April 2000 and December 2000, the S&P 500 fell 11%, and technology dropped 48%. During that same period, Varghese noted that utilities were up 46%, financials gained 23%, and consumer staples rose 41%.

Pointing to this historical period, Varghese warned that an increase in market breadth led by defensive stocks could be a negative signal for the market. “That was a rotation,” Varghese said. “I’m not saying we’re in that now, but that’s my ‘be careful what you wish for.'”

How Has the Stock Market Performed?

The S&P 500 index has advanced 12.81% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 17.43%, and the Dow Jones gained 8.98% YTD.

On Tuesday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ), which track the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, respectively, closed higher. SPY rose 0.56% to $769.66, while QQQ advanced 1.27% to $721.25. Meanwhile, the Dow tracker, State Street SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (NYSE:DIA), ended 0.059% higher at $523.28.

On Wednesday, SPY was up 0.36%, QQQ was 0.37% higher, and DIA rose 0.04%.

news.content:
Bill Ackman, the founder and CEO of Pershing Square USA, Ltd. (NYSE:PSUS), says investors should focus on businesses capable of creating significant value over decades, even when markets temporarily shut.

Ackman, during a podcast interview with Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management, published on Wednesday, said a great company was one investors could buy today and hold even if markets shut for two decades, with "an enormous degree of certainty" that they would own "something that’s enormously valuable" 10 or 20 years later.

He said his preferred businesses are not confined to a single industry. He compared them with royalty-collecting companies or annuities that can grow rapidly for extended periods without requiring substantial reinvestment.

To evaluate a potential investment, Ackman recommended finding the strongest short seller covering a company an investor owns and carefully examining that person’s case against it.

"Find the person who makes the best case for why you’re wrong," Ackman said. Investors should then decide whether those arguments alter their view or can be methodically rebutted.  “If you can rebut each of their arguments, then you can feel more confident in your investment,” he said.

Read Also: Bill Ackman and Elon Musk Both Want Dinner With the Same Founding Father

Ackman’s Checklist for Picking Winning Stocks

Pershing Square holds concentrated positions in companies including Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Brookfield Corp. (NYSE:BN), Uber Technologies Inc. (NYSE:UBER), Visa Inc.(NYSE:V) and Mastercard Inc. (NYSE:MA). Ackman said that while 200 to 300 businesses may qualify as truly great, fewer are available "at a price that makes it a great investment."

Ackman said investors often seek "get-rich-quick" strategies, while the asset management industry tends to be short-term focused, rather than taking a long-term view of businesses, as the legendary investor Warren Buffett does.

Ackman said Pershing Square uses a checklist to identify companies with durable competitive advantages and predictable long-term cash flows. He avoids businesses he cannot confidently value over 10–20 years and prioritizes business durability over short-term earnings, steering clear of companies highly exposed to external factors they cannot control such as commodity prices, interest rates or regulation. “We keep it simple,” he said.

Bill Ackman, who lost more than $400 million on Netflix Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX) in 2022 before exiting over concerns about its outlook, has returned to the stock, forecasting annualized returns "well into the 20s." He now calls Netflix a "high-growth utility," citing subscriber loyalty, pricing power and sustained earnings growth, and viewed its latest quarter favorably despite the post-earnings selloff. Netflix’s third-quarter operating income rose 37% to $4.46 billion, while cancellations declined despite price increases.

Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) shares are trading higher Wednesday in sympathy with SK Hynix Inc. (NASDAQ:SKHY), which reported record third-quarter results late Tuesday.

  • Micron stock is surging to new heights today. Why is MU stock up today?

SK Hynix Reports Record Profit, Revenue Above 100 Trillion Won and Sees Shortage Through 2030

SK Hynix reported third-quarter revenue of 104.62 trillion won ($78.8 billion), up 32% from the second quarter and above the 98.34 trillion won estimate, according to CNBC. It was the company’s first quarter with revenue above 100 trillion won. Operating profit was a record 83.33 trillion won, up 632% from a year earlier and above analysts’ estimate of about 76.7 trillion won, for an operating margin of about 80%.

SK Hynix said it expects demand for memory chips to exceed supply through 2030. DRAM made up 75% of revenue and NAND 24%, according to Investing.com. Net profit fell 58% from the second quarter to 39.78 trillion won because of non-operating losses. The company plans about 100 trillion won in shareholder returns for 2026, including a 20 trillion won share repurchase.

Why SK Hynix’s Results Are a Read-Through for Micron

Micron and SK Hynix make the same products, DRAM and high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, which goes into Nvidia Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)’s AI accelerators, so SK Hynix’s results speak to the same demand and pricing that drive Micron’s business. A record 80% operating margin and a shortage that SK Hynix expects to last through 2030 point to strong pricing across the industry. Samsung had also reported record preliminary third-quarter operating profit of 107.4 trillion won, according to TrendForce. Micron shares had slid earlier this month on concerns about growing competition from Chinese memory makers, according to MarketWatch, so the results also address worries about the sector’s outlook.

news.content:
As concerns about AI valuations and concentrated market leadership persist, investors looking to hedge an eventual selloff have options beyond betting directly against Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) or the Nasdaq-100.

Eric Balchunas, senior ETF analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, recently highlighted the AGF U.S. Market Neutral Anti-Beta Fund (NYSE:BTAL) as a potential hedge against an AI-driven downturn or a return of broader market participation. The fund shorts high-beta stocks and goes long low-beta stocks, seeking to profit from the relative performance gap.

But BTAL is just one approach. Investors can also reduce concentration risk, shift toward lower-volatility equities or hold short-term Treasuries without making an outright bearish bet on AI.

Five ETFs to Watch

1. BTAL: A Long-Short Hedge

BTAL offers a direct bet on the relative underperformance of high-beta stocks. However, its track record highlights the cost of getting the timing wrong. The fund lost 35.4% in the year ended June 30, 2026, while the S&P 500 gained 22.33%, according to its SEC-filed annual report. Its strategy can struggle when riskier stocks lead a rising market.

2. USMV: Lower-Volatility Equities

The iShares MSCI USA Min Vol Factor ETF (BATS:USMV) targets U.S. stocks with lower overall volatility. It lets you stay invested in equities while seeking a smoother ride, though it can still fall sharply during broad market selloffs.

3. RSP: Reduce Mega-Cap Concentration

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP) gives constituents approximately equal weight at each rebalance, unlike market-cap-weighted funds that allocate more to the biggest companies. If market leadership broadens beyond mega-cap technology, this approach could outperform concentrated benchmarks.

4. VTV: Rotate Toward Value

The Vanguard Value ETF (NYSE:VTV) provides exposure to U.S. value stocks. A rotation away from expensive growth shares could favor value, though the outcome depends on earnings, valuations and broader economic conditions.

5. SGOV: Park Money in Treasury Bills

The iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF (NYSE:SGOV) holds ultra-short U.S. Treasury securities. It offers a cash-like alternative for investors seeking to reduce equity exposure while retaining liquidity, rather than attempting to profit from a market decline.

The Catch: Hedging Isn’t Free

ETF flows suggest investors are diversifying, not abandoning AI. BlackRock reported that U.S.-listed ETFs attracted more than $1.5 trillion through September 2026. Technology remained the leading sector for equity inflows, while value ETFs gained ground on growth in September.

That divergence matters. Investors may want protection against an AI correction without giving up exposure to the technology spending cycle.

The key is matching the hedge to the risk. BTAL targets relative performance between high- and low-beta stocks; USMV changes equity exposure, RSP reduces concentration, VTV tilts toward value, and SGOV shifts money into short-term government debt.

None guarantees protection if markets fall. For investors, diversification may prove more durable than trying to predict exactly when the AI trade turns.

news.content:
Retirement investing is increasingly shifting toward generating regular cash flow, putting dividend-growth and covered-call ETFs in focus as investors seek income without abandoning equity-market exposure.

• What should traders watch with JEPI?

Options-Based ETFs Gain Ground

The options-based ETF market continues to expand. Nasdaq’s April 2026 research found that more than 800 U.S.-listed ETFs used options in their strategies, collectively managing over $250 billion in assets. Income-enhancement strategies, including covered calls, accounted for the largest share of assets in the segment.

Three funds illustrate different approaches to the retirement income trade: the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (NYSE:SCHD), JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF (NYSE:JEPI) and NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF (NASDAQ:QQQI).

SCHD, JEPI, QQQI Offer Different Income Strategies

SCHD focuses on dividend-paying U.S. companies, offering investors a more traditional income strategy. Schwab reported a 3.24% trailing 12-month distribution yield and a 3.13% 30-day SEC yield as of August and October, respectively. Its expense ratio stands at 0.06%, making it a relatively low-cost option for investors prioritizing dividend income and long-term equity exposure.

JEPI takes a different approach, combining large-cap U.S. stocks like Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT), Apple, Inc (NASDAQ:AAPL) and NVIDIA Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) with options strategies designed to generate monthly income. Its September fact sheet reported an 8.04% rolling 12-month dividend yield and a 0.35% expense ratio. The strategy also seeks lower volatility than the broader U.S. large-cap market.

QQQI targets investors seeking higher monthly distributions through Nasdaq-100 exposure and an actively managed call-option strategy. It has a 14.28% distribution rate alongside a negative 0.06% 30-day SEC yield. That difference underscores why headline distribution rates should not be confused with conventional investment yields. The fund also warns that distributions may include return of capital.

Investor Flows Highlight Continued Interest

Recent flows suggest continued investor interest. QQQI recorded cumulative inflows of $1.81 billion in the past three months, while SCHD recorded inflows of $9.78 billion, according to data accumulated by ETFDb. JEPI saw $252.11 million during the same period after a spell of ups and downs.

The Retirement Trade-Off: Income Today Versus Wealth Tomorrow

For retirees, the real test is whether an ETF can deliver sustainable income without undermining the portfolio needed to fund future expenses. High-distribution covered-call funds may help meet near-term spending needs, but capped upside, market losses and potential return-of-capital distributions can complicate long-term wealth preservation.

Investors approaching retirement should assess these funds against their withdrawal needs, inflation exposure and remaining investment horizon, rather than choosing solely on headline yields. The goal is not simply to generate more income today, but to ensure the money lasts throughout retirement.
